newsitem.title: USA: Fresh water should reach Mir in time, NASA says.
newsitem.headline: Fresh water should reach Mir in time, NASA says.

text.p: A senior NASA official said on Tuesday he expected fresh drinking water to reach Russia's Mir space station before its supply runs out in six to eight weeks.

The space shuttle Atlantis, tentatively scheduled for blastoff on Sept. 27, and an unmanned Russian cargo craft, set for launch the first week of October, are to deliver fresh water to Mir, said Frank Culbertson, who oversees NASA's missions to the space station.
"Both vehicles are available to replenish the Mir if needed and I think that is a good plan," he told a news conference.
The troubled space station is running low on water because much of its supplies were tainted earlier in the year by leaking anti-freeze from cooling systems.

If the station's water recycling systems are still contaminated, the station's water supply could run out as early as late September, but if the water is safe to drink there should be enough until early October, said Culbertson.
"The overall water situation in terms of how much is on board and how far it will stretch is something we are going to have to watch very carefully," he said.
Cosmonauts returning to earth this week will bring back samples of the recycled water for testing.
The new Mir crew will practice this weekend for a daring repair to restore some of the electrical power lost when the station's Spektr module was struck by an errant cargo craft in June.

During the internal spacewalk, planned for Aug. 20, Solovyev and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov would open up the airless compartment to tap the power from its solar panels. NASA astronaut Michael Foale will sit out the spacewalk in the station's Soyuz escape ship.

Restoration of the power will reactivate a badly needed spare oxygen generator. The station's primary oxygen generator has been broken since July 29 and the crew has had to rely on a chemical system for breathing air.

Culbertson said NASA was still considering a request from the Russian space authorities for Foale to assist Mir commander Anatoly Solovyev during a Sept. 3 spacewalk to inspect the crash-damaged Spektr module.
"We need to answer some of the concerns we have on safety and make sure we understand truly what the task would be," he said. "That's going to take another day or two probably."
Culbertson said Foale's participation in the spacewalk would provide engineers with a first hand account of the damage after he returns to Earth aboard the shuttle in early October.
"It would give Mike a chance to get up close and personal with the damaged areas and be a recent eyewitness when he comes back," he said.

The spacewalks will also look for other signs of damage on the station's exterior. Russian space officials now believe the out of control cargo craft may have scraped the station's main compartment before ploughing into the Spektr science module.
